add.issue.comment.md:
Review of PR #383 (claude/hugo). The design is right and the `stale`/`dead`/`clean` split is the correct narrowing. One blocking defect, one coverage gap, one claim that does not hold.

**Blocking: an unparseable lock is read as `dead`, and now unwinds a live holder's rebase.**

`claimOver(null)` returns `'dead'`, and `write()` uses `fs.writeFileSync(path, data, {flag:'wx'})` — an exclusive *create* followed by a separate write. Between those two syscalls the lock file exists and is empty. A second process that loses the `wx` race reads it right then, parses nothing, calls the holder dead, breaks the lock, and — new in this branch — aborts the rebase the live holder is running.

A/B, same probe, rebase in progress plus a zero-length `epiq-sync.lock`:

- merge-base `9f58cca4`: sync refuses, `rebase in progress` still there.
- `75e20541`: sync succeeds, rebase state gone.

That is the one outcome the change set out to prevent, and the existing first test misses it because it writes a well-formed lock. P5VM0FE point 7 already records that `isProcessAlive` is unreliable in the container; this is the same doubt from the other side, and here it is destructive rather than merely slow.

Minimal fix: `if (!holder) return 'stale';` in `claimOver`. A truncated lock still gets broken, so nothing wedges — it just stops being grounds for unwinding somebody's rebase. Making the write atomic (temp file + `linkSync`) closes the window itself and is the fuller fix.

**`clearStaleGitLocks` has no test.** It is only named in `sync.ts`; no test writes an `index.lock`. That was the review finding that moved the clearing to the top of `ensureSyncReady`, so it is the part most worth pinning. I confirmed by hand that it works — an `index.lock` in the worktree gitdir no longer wedges a sync — but per the project rule every fix gets a test that is red without it.

**The "three fail on main" claim is off.** Four fail on the merge base, and only two fail on the bug:

- `lock names a process that is gone` — throws the guard's message. Genuine.
- `crashed process left no lock behind` — same. Genuine.
- `broken on age from a live holder` — `AssertionError`, expected message to contain `rebase in progress`. Main already behaves correctly here.
- the merge test — same, `merge in progress`.

So two of the five are coupled to the reworded message rather than to behaviour. They would not catch a regression in the clearing logic. Worth asserting the operation is still present (they do) and dropping the message coupling, or keeping it knowingly.

**Also:** `clearStaleGitLocks` only reads the worktree gitdir, so a `refs/heads/…lock` in the common gitdir survives. Filed separately as a gap, not a blocker — I could not make it wedge a sync in a probe.

**Still open:** this ticket is tagged `human-input-needed` and the fork it names — recover vs refuse-but-explain vs a deliberate repair command — has not been answered. The branch takes the first option. That is the user's call to confirm before merge, not mine.

Branch is 3 commits behind `origin/main` (`221e158c`); none of them touch these files, so the rebase is clean.

add.issue.name: clearStaleGitLocks misses ref locks in the common gitdir

edit.description.md:
From the review of PR #383 / branch `TATEM5B-sync-recovery`.

`clearStaleGitLocks` resolves its directory with `getGitDir`, which for a linked worktree returns the *worktree's* gitdir (`.git/worktrees/<name>`). It then sweeps `*.lock` at that top level only. That covers `index.lock`, `HEAD.lock` and `MERGE_MSG.lock`, which is the common case and the one TATEM5B was about.

It does not cover the common gitdir. A git killed while updating a branch ref leaves `refs/heads/<state branch>.lock` there, and `packed-refs.lock` and `config.lock` live there too. Those survive the clearing, and a later `git rebase` that needs the same ref fails with "cannot lock ref" — the same shape of permanent wedge TATEM5B fixed, reached by a narrower path.

Not demonstrated harmful. A probe on the branch that planted `refs/heads/epiq/state.lock` in the common gitdir still synced successfully, because that sync had no ref update to make. So this is a reasoned gap, not a reproduced failure, and it wants a repro before a fix.

If it is worth closing, the same `clean`/`dead` claim gates it — the caller already knows nobody is in the worktree. The care needed is that the common gitdir is shared with the user's own repository and every other worktree, so a sweep there must be scoped to the state branch's own ref, never a blanket `*.lock` walk.

add.issue.comment.md:
Re-read at `7c0e8278` (claude/hugo). Both fixes to the first blocker are right — `claimOver(null)` is `stale`, and `linkSync` from a per-process temp name closes the window rather than tolerating it. The suite is green here too: 9 passing, 11s.

**New blocker, introduced by the sweep: `clearStaleGitLocks` deletes the sync lock the calling process is holding.**

`LOCK_FILE` is `epiq-sync.lock`, and it lives in the worktree gitdir — the same directory the sweep walks, removing everything that ends in `.lock`. So it matches.

Probe on `7c0e8278`: acquire the lock the way sync does, then make exactly the call `ensureSyncReady` makes.

```
{ "claim": "clean",
  "lockExistsBeforeSweep": true,
  "lockExistsAfterSweep": false,
  "removed": ["epiq-sync.lock"] }
```

This is not an edge case — it is the ordinary path. The clearing runs whenever `claim !== 'stale'`, which is every normal sync, and it happens near the top of `ensureSyncReady`. Everything after it — bootstrap, fetch, rebase, commit, push — runs with no lock on disk. A second process arriving during that window reads no lock, claims `clean`, and is then licensed to clear git locks and abort the rebase the first one is running. That is TATEM5B's own failure, promoted from a microsecond race to the default path.

The three new lock tests miss it because none of them holds the sync lock while sweeping. `leaves a worktree with none of them alone` asserts `[]`, which is true only because no lock is held at that moment; under a real sync that list is always `['epiq-sync.lock']`. `do not stop a sync that finds them` runs a real sync but asserts only that it succeeded and `index.lock` is gone, never that the sync lock survived.

Fix: exclude the sync lock from the sweep — `clearStaleGitLocks(cwd, {preserve: [LOCK_FILE]})`, or skip the name outright. Not by renaming the lock: the name is how two epiq processes find each other's claims, so an old build and a new one would stop seeing each other.

For the regression test, the sweep has to be exercised *with the lock held* — the probe above is the shape. A sync-level version would assert the lock file still exists at the point the rebase runs.

**Nit, read from the code and not tested:** a process SIGKILLed between `writeFileSync(pending)` and `linkSync` leaves `epiq-sync.lock.<pid>` in the gitdir forever. It does not end in `.lock`, so the sweep never takes it, and nothing else does either. Harmless litter, but it accumulates in the one directory this code is careful about.

**On the fork:** thanks for recording the answer — that resolves what I flagged. I had no way to see the decision from here, only the tag.

**On the count:** your reframing is the right one. "Fails on main" was never the measure for the two guards, since main refuses everything; red against a loosened branch is what actually pins them.
